Hormuz: Qatar takes an Iranian plan to the White House, $8 billion in exchange for reopening the strait, and oil falls

On Monday, November 9, Qatar's prime minister presented Donald Trump and JD Vance with an Iranian plan: Tehran would reopen Hormuz if Washington lifted its blockade and released $8 billion in frozen assets. Nothing is signed, the nuclear issue is a sticking point, and ships were hit again this weekend [1][2][3].

On Monday, November 9, Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, was due to meet President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance in Washington, carrying an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz [1][2].

According to diplomatic sources cited by the press, Iran would reopen the strait and stop attacking Gulf tankers; the United States would lift its naval and economic blockade and release $8 billion in frozen Iranian assets held in Qatar [2]. Iran would give up controlling the strait and charging transit fees there, but still refuses to put its nuclear programme on the table [2][4]. The White House has confirmed nothing [2].
On November 6, Qatar had already handed over a two-step plan spread over 48 hours, which adds a nuclear component from day one with inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) [4].

On Sunday, Trump called new American strikes "very unlikely" if the talks led to a solid deal, while keeping the military "ready to fire" [5]. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for his part, called Iran's demands "outrageous and ridiculous" and said the two sides were not close to a breakthrough [2].

On the water, the situation remains tense: the Revolutionary Guards said on November 8 that navigation aids in the south of the strait had been destroyed and that no unauthorised vessel had passed through overnight [3]. They also said three tankers had caught fire in what they call an illegal channel, without naming the ships or providing verifiable evidence [6].
On the market, Brent lost 3.6% on Monday to end around $94 a barrel, according to one reading [2]; another site reports a fall of nearly 5% during the session [1].

Key takeaway: oil is falling on hope of a deal, not on a deal. Traders are betting that a "strait reopened in exchange for blockade lifted" swap is possible, but analysts note that prices are falling on promises, not on concrete progress [1][2].

The mechanism is simple: every rumour of Hormuz reopening takes a risk premium off a barrel, while every tanker hit puts it back. The $8 billion is the key bargaining chip: these are Iranian assets that sanctions prevent Tehran from spending, and it wants them before reopening [2].

The past calls for caution: a US-Iran memorandum concluded in Switzerland in May collapsed after an Iranian attack on tankers in the strait [1]. Today, the blockage comes from the nuclear issue: Washington wants inspections from day one, Tehran wants to keep that file separate [4].

For you in France, what is being played out in Doha and Washington shows up at the pump and on your gas bill: when Brent drops 3 or 4% in a day, wholesale fuel prices tend to follow. But as long as the strait is not truly reopened, the easing can reverse as fast as it did this weekend.

China: exports jump 35% in October, driven by chips and cars, and this year's surplus already exceeds $1 trillion

Chinese customs announced on Tuesday, November 10, that exports rose 35.2% year on year in October, and imports 41.6%. The month's surplus falls to $105.3 billion, but the ten-month surplus reaches $1.04 trillion, a month earlier than in 2025 [1][2][3].
In October, Chinese exports grew 35.2% year on year in dollar terms, more than the 33.5% expected by economists polled by Reuters, but slightly less than September's 36.3% [1].
Imports jumped 41.6%, well above the roughly 32% expected and September's 31%; high-tech imports rose 72% in value according to CNBC's calculation [1][2].

October's trade surplus comes to $105.3 billion, against $133.5 billion in September, its lowest level since April; over January-October it reaches around $1.04 trillion, more than 8% higher than a year earlier, and crosses the $1 trillion mark for the second year running, a month earlier than in 2025 [1][2][3].

Sales to the European Union rose 24.4% while purchases of European products fell by more than 4%, which widens China's surplus with the EU to $33.4 billion; sales to the United States climbed 32.9%, for a surplus of $32.7 billion [1][2].

Car sales on the Chinese market fell for a twelfth month in a row, while vehicle exports are rising: carmakers are making up abroad for weak domestic demand [2][3]. A year earlier, in October 2025, exports had on the contrary fallen and those to the United States had dropped 25%, which inflates the comparison [4].
Key takeaway: China is selling more and more to the world while its own people spend little, and this imbalance is turning into trade tension with Europe and the United States [1][2].

The good surprise hides an explanation: the rise in imports comes largely from components and materials linked to building data centres for artificial intelligence, and higher commodity prices also play a part, according to the analyses cited [2][3]. The figure is therefore less a sign of strong domestic demand than of a global technology cycle.

Politically, the timing is sensitive: the European Union reached a deal with Beijing last month to limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles for a few years [1], and Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are due to meet at the APEC summit in China [3]. A lower October surplus may soften criticism a little, but the year's total is still heading for a record [2][3].
At Moody's, economist Dave Chia expects solid exports through the end of the year, driven by electronics and cars [2].

For you, this surplus explains why Europe is taking a harder line on Chinese electric and hybrid cars: when Chinese sales to Europe rise 24% in a year while purchases of European products fall, European factories are directly affected.

Ukraine: Russians, Ukrainians and Americans meet in Abu Dhabi for the first time since February, with the Donbas standing in the way

On Tuesday, November 10, delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened three-way talks in Abu Dhabi, the first since the Geneva meeting of February 18. Europeans are kept away from the table, and Moscow still demands all of the Donbas [1][2][3].

The negotiations open on Tuesday, November 10, in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, under American mediation; they are due to continue on the 11th [1][2]. It is the first three-way meeting since the one in Geneva on February 18; rounds had already been held in Abu Dhabi in January and February [2][5].

The United States is represented by envoy Steve Witkoff and by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, who are to get the two sides talking [1][3]. On the Ukrainian side, the delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, who stresses coordination with European partners [1][5].

Moscow has unveiled a team led by Vladimir Medinsky, according to AFP [1]; Meduza also lists in the delegation deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov [5].

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov repeats that these are three-way negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with American mediation, and Russia does not want Europeans to take part in the discussion on ending the conflict [1][2][3]. British, French, German and Italian officials, as well as NATO and European Commission representatives, are therefore holding separate meetings with the Ukrainians in Abu Dhabi [1][3].

On substance, Russia continues to demand that Ukraine cede the whole of the Donbas [1]. A senior American official says both sides have privately signalled they are ready for territorial compromises [2].

Volodymyr Zelensky says his army's recent successes and heavy Russian losses strengthen his position; the front has barely moved for months, however, and Russian commanders deny any Ukrainian reconquest [2]. Kyrylo Budanov, described as the president's chief of staff, says Kyiv will focus first on prisoner exchanges and humanitarian issues [2].

Key takeaway: after nine months without a three-way table, the resumption is a fact in itself, but nobody is announcing a breakthrough, and the issue that has blocked things from the start, the Donbas, remains untouched [1][2].

The context weighs on the talks: Zelensky has warned of a possible new large-scale Russian strike on energy and logistics, and a local truce negotiated in an occupied city ended on Sunday [5]. The bombardments of recent days on the Ukrainian power grid are a reminder that military pressure continues while diplomats talk.
The absence of Europeans is the second sensitive point: they would be the first to be affected by any post-war security guarantees, but they only have access to parallel meetings [1][3].

For you, the stakes are concrete: a deal, even a partial one, on security or energy would affect gas and electricity prices in Europe and France's defence budget. For now nothing is settled: the talks cover security, de-escalation and the humanitarian side.

news.2026-11-10-japon-boj-hausse-decembr: Japan: the Bank of Japan debates speeding up rate hikes, and December becomes the date to watch, with the yen around 158 to the dollar

The summary of opinions of the Bank of Japan, published on Tuesday, November 10, shows that some of its members want to raise rates faster after October's pause at 1.25%. Markets give about a 70% chance of a hike in December, while the yen stays near 158 to the dollar [1][2][3][4].

On November 10, the Bank of Japan published the summary of opinions from its October meeting: the debate is now less about whether to raise rates than about the pace, after the policy rate was held at 1.25% [1][2].

October's decision was taken by 8 votes to 1: Hajime Takata voted against holding and proposed 1.5% [2]. In September, the bank had raised its rate to 1.25%, a 31-year high, by 7 votes to 2; two members appointed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had voted against [5].

One committee member considers the neutral rate, the one that neither restrains nor stimulates the economy, to be "well above 1%"; another warns on the contrary that with the rate already in the neutral zone, another hike could weigh on activity, against a backdrop of weak household spending [3][4].
Governor Kazuo Ueda said a further hike in December was possible, and traders cited by Bloomberg give it about a 70% chance [2][6].

On the market, the yen was little changed around 158 to the dollar, and the finance minister warned that the government would act "very quickly" in case of currency volatility [7]. The Nikkei rebounded 2.6% to 2.8% on Tuesday, to around 60,300 to 60,500 points, after a fall of nearly 6% on Friday on fears of a slowdown in artificial intelligence investment [7].

Key takeaway: the more rates rise in Japan, the more attractive the yen becomes and the higher the cost of borrowing for the state and for companies. A hike in December would be the second in three months [2][5].

The dilemma is one of dosage: underlying inflation has reached the bank's 2% target, but consumption remains soft and the strength of AI-related demand is uncertain, as this week's falls on the Tokyo stock market showed [3][7].
The weak yen, near 158, makes energy imports more expensive in the middle of the Gulf crisis; the 160 yen per dollar mark is mentioned as a limit not to be crossed [7].

For you, a rate rise in Japan can have effects well beyond Tokyo: the yen has long served as a cheap funding currency for investors around the world, and when it strengthens they may sell other assets. It is one of the threads linking Japan to European markets.
The Bank of Japan meets again; a hike to 1.5% is considered by some analysts [2][6].

Saudi Arabia: the Houthis target the Aramco tower in the heart of Riyadh, and the Yemen war moves closer to the kingdom's finances

On Sunday, November 8, debris from intercepted Houthi missiles shattered windows on several floors of an Aramco tower in Riyadh's financial district, with no casualties. The Yemeni rebels say they also targeted the airport and oil tanks; the Saudi economy is already shrinking [1][2][3][4].

On Sunday, November 8, debris from intercepted missiles damaged a building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District: windows on several floors of the tower blew out, and the Energy Ministry said there were no casualties [1][2][3].

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles launched by the Houthis toward the capital; it then says it destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Saada, Yemen [3][5].

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree describes a coordinated series of strikes against the financial district, Riyadh's international airport, Aramco oil tanks and the town of Abqaiq, in the east of the country; Riyadh says it is examining these claims [3].

Qatar, Bahrain and Syria condemned the attacks [5]. According to the New York Times, attacks have been taking place almost daily in Riyadh for a few weeks, while Saudi forces continue their strikes in Yemen [3].
On Tuesday, November 10, Saudi Arabia again shot down missiles fired toward Riyadh after a Houthi attack on a pipeline, according to Al Jazeera [4].

The group is holding up nonetheless: Aramco announced on November 3 a third-quarter profit up about 35%, thanks to a barrel sold at an average of $95.20 against $70.10 a year earlier, and it kept exporting through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu [6].

Key takeaway: the attack is more symbolic than destructive, but it hits the kingdom's financial centre just as the regional war weighs on its accounts. The Saudi Finance Ministry expects the economy to shrink by 3.6% in 2026, and the IMF a contraction of 3.3% [6].

The mechanism is a double shock: expensive oil swells Aramco's profits, but the blocked Strait of Hormuz forces the country to use the East-West pipeline, precisely the one targeted by the Houthis, and the attacks on Riyadh worry investors and airlines [4][6]. In October, Aramco chief Amin Nasser had warned that rebuilding global oil stocks could take up to two years and that the safety margin was "dreadfully thin" [7].
Yemen thus becomes a second front in the conflict surrounding Iran: what is decided in Doha and Washington on Hormuz does not necessarily settle the Houthi threat to the Gulf [3][4].

For you, it is a reminder that oil does not only pass through Hormuz: the Red Sea, the Saudi pipeline and drone attacks matter too. If Gulf exports are disrupted on several sides at once, petrol and diesel stay expensive in Europe, even when Brent falls.

news.2026-11-10-turquie-inflation-livre-: Turkey: inflation picks up to 29.77% and the lira crosses 50 to the dollar, a week before the central bank's report

Turkish inflation reached 29.77% year on year in October, slightly more than expected, as the lira crossed 50 to the dollar for the first time. The central bank publishes its quarterly inflation report on Thursday, November 12 [1][2][3].
Annual inflation rose to 29.77% in October, from 29.73% in September, which was a near five-year low; analysts had expected 29.56% [1][2].
In October alone, prices rose 2.58%, against 1.84% in September; the independent group ENAG measures inflation of 45.12% over one year [1].

On October 22, the central bank, led by Fatih Karahan, had cut its policy rate from 37% to 36%, its first cut in nine months, while warning that higher energy prices were weighing on inflation [3][4].

Key takeaway: Turkey is cutting rates while inflation picks up, and the currency is on a slow downward slope: the lira traded around 50 to the dollar in early November, a record, with a loss of about 19% over twelve months [5].

The central bank has to balance supporting the economy against defending the currency, while oil made expensive by the Gulf raises the energy bill of an importing country. It publishes its fourth and last inflation report of the year on November 12, and meets again on December 10 [2][3].
For you, a weaker lira makes Turkey cheaper to visit and its goods cheaper to export; but for Turks, it means eroding purchasing power.

news.2026-11-10-syrie-arabie-saoudite-pa: Syria: Damascus denies sending troops to Yemen, but its defence pact with Riyadh is already fuelling talk of military aid against the Houthis

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani assured on Monday, November 9, that Syria has no soldiers in Yemen and no plan to send any. The defence pact signed on November 4 with Saudi Arabia provides, he says, for no deployment [1][2][3].

On Monday, November 9, Asaad al-Shaibani declared that Syria had no troops in Yemen and no plan, in the short term, to send any; the military agreement with Riyadh aims to rebuild the Syrian army [1][2].

The agreement was signed on November 4 during Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's visit to Riyadh; it covers advisory, training and expertise-sharing support, and the visit also produced six concessional loans worth more than $403 million from the Saudi Fund for Development to rebuild Syria [3][4].

Contradictory reports are circulating: Reuters reported, citing Syrian and American sources, that Damascus had sent military advisers and training teams to Saudi Arabia, and AP mentioned about 600 special forces soldiers due to deploy, mainly on the Yemeni border; AFP even reported that Syrians would run drone operations against the Houthis in Yemen, which Damascus denies [2][3][4][5].

Key takeaway: by rebuilding its army with Saudi help, Syria is moving closer to Riyadh's camp while the Houthis strike the Saudi capital almost every day [3][5]. The minister also said he was studying joining the joint Mecca defence pact, which already binds Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, without this being confirmed [4].
The denial is calibrated: advising and training Saudis is not fighting in Yemen, a nuance that matters for a country seeking funding to rebuild [3][4].

For you, Syria is becoming an actor in Gulf security, which matters for regional stability and for oil routes; Saudi loans can also ease reconstruction projects that European companies might be interested in.

news.2026-11-10-thailande-pib-troisieme-: Thailand: third-quarter GDP is due on November 15 or 16, and the Prime Minister disputes the official agency's growth forecast

Bangkok will publish its third-quarter growth in mid-November. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul disputes the official agency NESDC's 2.1% forecast, whose chief denies having been ordered to inflate the figures; Thailand remains the weakest in Southeast Asia [1][2][3].
According to economic calendars, third-quarter GDP is due to be published on November 15 (Bangkok time) or November 16 depending on the time zone used [2].
In the second quarter, growth was 1.9% year on year, against 1.7% expected and 2.8% in the first quarter; the NESDC agency forecast in August 2% to 2.5% for 2026 [2][3].
On October 28, Prime Minister Anutin disputed the 2.1% forecast, citing stronger indicators, and NESDC secretary-general Danucha Pichayanan denied having been ordered to inflate the figures [1].

Key takeaway: Thailand, which saw growth of 1.2% in the third quarter of 2025, is the slowest-growing of the major Southeast Asian economies, according to the October IMF, which sees Vietnam at 8.4% and the Philippines at 3.4% [4][5].

The debate over the figures is sensitive: the government needs good news, and the official agency must prove its independence. The mid-November release will show whether methodological corrections really change the growth measured [1].
For you, Thailand is a major trading partner and travel destination in Asia; weak growth measured in a disputed way is a reminder that official figures themselves can become a political stake.
